flawed_step: Step 8: the alternating preference cycle does not contradict stability; different participants may have cyclically opposed preferences.
counterexample: Let n=2 with preferences m1: w1>w2; m2: w2>w1; w1: m2>m1; w2: m1>m2. Both {(m1,w1),(m2,w2)} and {(m1,w2),(m2,w1)} are stable and distinct.
assessment_summary:
1. Let M and N be two stable matchings in an arbitrary instance. — Justified: this is the appropriate setup for attempting to prove uniqueness.
2. Assume M≠N and choose a man m0 whose partners differ between M and N. — Justified: distinct perfect matchings must assign some man different partners.
3. Write w0=M(m0), and, after interchanging M and N if necessary, suppose m0 prefers w0 to N(m0). — Justified: preferences are strict and complete, so m0 strictly prefers one of his two distinct partners.
4. Let m1 be w0's partner in N. Stability of N implies that w0 prefers m1 to m0. — Justified: otherwise (m0,w0) would block N, since m0 prefers w0 to his N-partner.
5. Stability of M implies that m1 prefers his M-partner w1=M(m1) to w0. — Justified: w0 prefers m1 to her M-partner m0, so (m1,w0) would block M unless m1 preferred w1 to w0.
6. Repeating Steps 4–5 produces an alternating sequence in which each man prefers his M-partner to his N-partner and each encountered woman prefers her N-partner to her M-partner. — Justified: the same stability argument applies at every stage, and strict preferences ensure the relevant partners differ.
7. Because the instance is finite, this sequence eventually repeats and therefore contains an alternating cycle. — Justified: only finitely many participants exist.
8. Claim that such an alternating cycle contradicts stability. — Not justified: its comparisons belong to different participants and are entirely compatible with both matchings being stable.
9. Conclude from Step 8 that M=N and hence that the stable matching is unique. — Not justified: it depends on the false claim in Step 8.
10. To test the failed inference, take n=2 with m1: w1>w2; m2: w2>w1; w1: m2>m1; and w2: m1>m2. — Justified: these are strict, complete preference orderings.
11. Define A={(m1,w1),(m2,w2)}. — Justified: A is a matching covering all participants.
12. A is stable. — Justified: in the only unmatched pairs, m1 does not prefer w2 to w1 and m2 does not prefer w1 to w2, so neither blocks A.
13. Define B={(m1,w2),(m2,w1)}. — Justified: B is another matching covering all participants.
14. B is stable. — Justified: for (m1,w1), w1 prefers her partner m2; for (m2,w2), w2 prefers her partner m1. Thus neither unmatched pair blocks B.
15. Since A and B are distinct stable matchings in one permitted instance, the statement is false. — Justified: this directly refutes the asserted uniqueness.
